- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

{"number":1264,"title":"Delete the two-name settings-file tolerance once no member carries .claudinite-checks.json","body":"Phase 3 of #1252. The rename landed with every reader in the corpus accepting **both** settings-file names, because a member renames its own file only on the converge that carries `engine/migrations/2026-08-23-settings-file-rename`. This issue is the removal of that tolerance.

## The precondition — a converge-cycle fact, never a date

Do not open this on a calendar. The condition is: **no member still carries `.claudinite-checks.json`**, confirmed by reading the fleet's own artifacts rather than assumed from elapsed time. Retiring a tolerance while a member is still on the old shape does not just leave that member behind — every reader then finds no settings file at all, which reads as "declares no packs, never adopted", silently, with green runs to show for it (the same class as #1106).

The sheepdog roster walk already reads each member's declaration under both names, so the cheapest confirmation is to have it report which name each member answered on.

## What comes out

- `engine/settings-file.mjs`: `LEGACY_SETTINGS_FILE`, and `SETTINGS_FILES` collapses to the one name. Everything downstream that maps over it becomes a single path.
- `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs`: `LEGACY_CONFIG_KEYS` (`claudinite`, `maintenance`) and the two fold-in branches that read them — the legacy `packVersions` map, `claudinite.engineVersion`, and `maintenance.delivery` → `dailyClaudiniteUpdatesRequirePrReview`. A member still declaring either then gets the unknown-setting error, which is correct once none does.
- `engine/installed-versions.mjs`: `LEGACY_STAMP_KEY` and its read path.
- `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs`: `LEGACY_ENDPOINTS_KEY`, and `SCHEDULE_KEYS` drops `endpoints`.
- `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`: `resolveDelivery`, `deliveryFromChecks`, and `deliveryFor`'s `maintenance.delivery` fallback — gated separately on no fielded vendored worker still importing them (walk the trunk's pack history, per the `updates/*` rule).
- `engine/served-by.mjs`: same gate, same walk. Nothing in canon calls it now.
- The both-name reads in `fleet-api.mjs`, `fleet-reads.mjs`, `signals/fleet.mjs`, `packs/claudinite-dashboard/settings-read.mjs`, `seeds-agree.mjs`, `adopt-pack/checks.mjs`, `selftest.mjs`, and the older migration records that read the declaration.
- The `legacy-settings-name` rehearsal fixture, and the assertion in `rehearsal.test.mjs` that requires exactly one fixture to carry the retired name.
- The retired name in the two `except` lists (`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/declared-checks.json`, `packs/product-wiki/declared-checks.json`), the dashboard stub's `paths:`/`hashFiles`, and the `find` in `environment-setup-command.sh`.

The last three are the ones to check by hand rather than by grep: a stub is copied into a member once and never re-copied, and the setup script is pasted into a container by hand, so both outlive a member's converge by an unknown margin. They come out last, or not at all.

{"number":276,"title":"Move chrome-extension-release plumbing out of core `.github/` into the pack (vendored into consumers)","body":"Resolves the **RELEASE** item of #270: the reusable release workflows (`.github/workflows/chrome-extension-*.yml` + `deploy-privacy-page.yml`) and the three composite actions (`read-release-config`, `bump-extension-patch`, `report-failure`) live in Claudinite's core tree but exist solely for the `chrome-extension-release` pack. They must move behind the pack that owns them, leaving Claudinite with no release-specific GitHub Actions.

## Decision (agreed with owner)

- **Hosting model: vendor into each consumer.** GitHub only resolves reusable workflows/composite actions from a repo's own `.github/`, never from a `packs/…` subdir, so "into the pack" means the pack holds the templates and each consumer hosts a *managed* copy in its own `.github/`. Consumers become self-contained; baselining (not the consumer) owns keeping the copies correct. This reverses the original "thin consumer" design — deliberately.
- **Phase-2 deletion: automatic, telemetry-gated.** Once the fleet census confirms every consumer has vendored, the census deletes Claudinite's release plumbing automatically as part of migration retirement — no follow-up PR.
- **Secrets: nothing to migrate.** The four `CHROME_*` secrets already live in each consumer repo (they travel via `secrets: inherit` from the consumer's own workflow); Claudinite holds none.

## Plan

1. **Pack = source of truth.** Move the 4 workflows + 3 composite actions into `packs/chrome-extension-release/` as vendored templates; rewrite cross-repo `uses: missingbulb/Claudinite/.github/…@main` → local `uses: ./.github/…`; rename to avoid the in-repo filename collision (the orchestrator and the create-package reusable are both `chrome-extension-release.yml` today).
2. **Migration is the fix vehicle.** A new baseline migration carries: (a) a **materialize** op — baselining writes the vendored set into each consumer's `.github/` and drops the old thin-stub `@main` refs; (b) a **legacyPresent** probe ("still references `missingbulb/Claudinite/.github/workflows/chrome-extension-*`") for fleet telemetry; (c) a **retire-deletes-from-home** list — Claudinite's own release files. Extend the migration mechanism (today rename-only) with the materialize op, and teach the census to delete the home-repo files on retirement.
3. **Tolerant checks during transition.** The `cer/*` checks accept both the old thin-stub shape and the new vendored shape until the migration retires, so no consumer's check suite goes red mid-flight.
4. **Docs.** Update `RELEASE.md`, `.github/workflows/README.md` (drop the frozen-`@main`-API section), and the pack fingerprint.

## Prerequisite for the automatic cut

The automatic phase-2 deletion needs `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` granted **Contents-write on the home repo** — #239 notes this is not granted yet. Until it is, the census logs "grant FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN Contents write" and Claudinite's copies stay in place (harmless — consumers already run off their vendored copies by then).

Refs #270 (RELEASE item), #239 (token scope).","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/276","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["blocked"],"assignees":[],"comments":5,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-07-13T14:28:14Z","updated_at":"2026-08-22T05:13:24Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```

We hit the same wall from the other side (Desktop scheduled tasks, 6 machines), and there is one property of the platform that may unblock you without waiting on Anthropic.

Approvals are stored **on the scheduled task**, not on the run and not on the settings file. The app says so in its own `create_scheduled_task` / `update_scheduled_task` tool result:

> Tool approvals granted during a run are stored on the task and auto-applied to future runs.

So for a prompt that a scheduler cannot click, the workaround is to click it **once, by hand, on a task you then never throw away**:

1. create the routine task once and run it manually ("Run now") with a human present — approve the Workflow opt-in there;
2. from then on never create a fresh task for that job. Re-point the same warm task at new work with `update_scheduled_task(taskId=…, prompt=…, description=…, fireAt=…)`. Measured on our side today: the update path raises no dialog at all, and a one-time task fires immediately (the several-minute dispatch delay applies only to recurring ones);
3. if you worry the reused task shows up under a stale name — have the seed prompt call `set_session_title` on its first turn. Verified: the session then appears under its real name (`titleSource: tool`).

The catch worth knowing before you build on it: it is per-task and invisible. A new task is cold and re-asks for everything, and nothing tells you which of your tasks are cold until one stalls. That part is auditable from disk — each task-spawned session records `scheduledTaskId` and `permissionMode` in `local_.json` next to the task store, so a nightly check can name the tasks that will stall before they do: https://gist.github.com/tonydzi/64183d29eeaa37d7b38a3775012a8c1d (stdlib only, read-only, CC0).

Not a fix for the gate itself — the ask in this issue stays valid. But it may move you from "blocked, waiting on upstream" to "runs unattended, with one human click per task, ever."

{"number":1133,"title":"converge-item.mjs needs a real GITHUB_TOKEN the queue's own sessions don't have","body":"`engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md` step 6 tells every work-item session to converge by running:

```bash
node /scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue  --outcome ... --summary '...'
```

`converge-item.mjs` reads and writes the issue over a direct `api.github.com` fetch, authenticated with `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN` (`engine/scheduler/signals/gh.mjs`). That's fine for the retired executor mechanism, which ran as the Action's own job step with `GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}` set in its shell (`.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`). But the sessions the *current* queue dispatches to are Claude Code cloud/web sessions (`claude.ai/code/session_...`, per the hand-off comment on each work item) — and that session type's platform policy is MCP-only GitHub access: no `gh` CLI, no direct API calls. The `GITHUB_TOKEN` such a session does see in its shell env is not a GitHub credential at all (14 chars, `prox...` prefix — a proxy artifact), so the script's very first call (`readIssue`) fails with a 401 before it ever reaches its own judgment logic.

Hit this converging #1129 (implementing #1124): `GITHUB_REPOSITORY=missingbulb/Claudinite node engine/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue 1129 --outcome done --summary '...'` exited 1 with `converge-item: #1129 could not be read`. Worked around it by replicating the script's side effects (comment with the same `claudinite-task-exec` record line, `task:agent`→`task:done` swap, close as completed) directly over the `mcp__github__*` tools instead — same end state, just not "in code" as instructed. Skipped only the `readyDependents` release, which `readiness.mjs` itself documents as safe to skip for a close performed outside the script (the hourly scheduler run is the backstop).

The retired `executor.md` already solved the same problem for a different script shape: its `needs-issue` verdict has the session fetch the one issue it needs over MCP, save the raw JSON, and hand it to the shell via `--issue-json ` rather than have the shell fetch it itself. `converge-item.mjs` has no such path — it only ever fetches and writes live. Given it writes too (comment, label, close), an `--issue-json` equivalent alone wouldn't fully solve it; it'd need either a write-side MCP shim as well, or a documented "no working token → do these exact steps over your GitHub tools instead" fallback in `instructions.md` step 6, mirroring what every session hitting this will otherwise rediscover from scratch.

Every future `implement-request` (and any other queue task converging through this same step 6) will hit this identically in this session type — this isn't specific to #1124/#1129.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1133","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["quick-win"],"assignees":[],"comments":3,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-20T22:03:49Z","updated_at":"2026-08-22T05:12:13Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1096,"title":"Every executor run logs `could not reconcile label "claude-automerge": 404`","body":"Every executor run on canon prints this before doing anything:

```
! could not reconcile label "claude-automerge": 404
```

Seen on `main`'s run [32368276774](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32368276774/job/96422660810) and on a branch run of #1089 at the same minute, so it is **not** from that PR — it is standing behavior on every run, and has been long enough that nobody reads the line any more.

`ensureLabels(gh, repo, [...QUEUE_LABELS, ...REQUEST_LABELS])` is the caller; `AUTOMERGE_LABEL` (`claude-automerge`) is in `REQUEST_LABELS`. The reconcile is fail-soft, which is why the run stays green — but the label is the asker's merge authorization (`MERGE_IF_NARROW`), read from a write-gated label at adoption. A label that cannot be reconciled is one that may not exist in the picker for a person to apply, which would make that authorization unreachable rather than merely unstamped.

Worth establishing before deciding the fix:

- whether the label exists on the repo at all, or the 404 is the *update* path failing on a label that does exist,
- whether the same line appears on members (it would be the same code, so probably),
- whether anything has ever successfully read `claude-automerge` off an issue here.

Filed rather than fixed in #1089 because it is unrelated to that diff, and a fail-soft warning nobody has acted on is exactly the kind that earns its own change.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1096","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["quick-win"],"assignees":[],"comments":1,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-20T12:22:00Z","updated_at":"2026-08-21T04:29:46Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

Three decisions this slice made that the plan left open, all reviewable in the PR:

1. **A pack's `tasks/` folder rides the tasks pack**, not the pack that owns the task. That is what keeps closure true for `basics`, `claudinite-lifecycle` and `claudinite-growth` without any of them declaring `requires: ['claudinite-tasks']` — which would have made the tasks pack universal and contradicted §18. 3. **The shims need more than a re-export.** A command-line entry decides it is the program by comparing `import.meta.url` to `process.argv[1]`; reached through a shim, that comparison fails and `node .../engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs` would define exports and exit 0. `engine/scheduler/legacy-entry.mjs` rewrites the path first, and every shim imports it before its re-export.

Also deferred out of PR A: `implement-request` stays a built-in under `queue/tasks/` rather than becoming an ordinary pack task — that changes its wire id, so it belongs with the decode work, not the move.

#1326 merged, and **the canary immediately failed on the merge commit** — which is exactly what it is for. Details and the fix in #1334 / #1335.

The defect: the `engine/scheduler/` shims are engine-lane files that re-export a pack, and the two lanes deliver on separate cycles. A member converging its engine first held a shim pointing at a pack its mount did not carry yet; the pack version it still had imports `engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs` by name; the pack failed to load; the self-test gate refused to land the converge — which also meant the member could not receive the pack that would have fixed it.

Reproduced against the real `ClaudiniteCanary` clone, not a fixture, and fixed by shipping `packs/claudinite-tasks/` in the engine lane for as long as the shims exist. The canary is green on the fix branch, with the workflow's own anti-vacuous guard confirming it converged:

```
update: engine — ok: the converged tree passed its self-test
update: packs  — ok: the converged tree passed its self-test
claudinite-rehearsal: converged missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary against  — merge
```

Also verified on that clone: the member's own vendored `check_the_world` exits 0, its declaration picks up `claudinite-tasks` from the seeding record, and the exact `run:` line its workflow carries — `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs` — still executes as the program through the shim and prints its run report. That last one is the L2-window risk, now observed rather than argued.

**Why this could not be watched now.** The two halves of the change reach a member on different clocks. The mount refreshes on a converge; `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` is the one path a converge cannot push, so it lands later as a pull request somebody merges. The window this shim exists for — **new mount, old workflow, still naming `tick.mjs`** — therefore only opens once a member has converged, and is only exercised at that member's next hourly scheduler run. At the time of writing GoogleCalendarEventCreator had the old mount and the old workflow, so the window had not opened yet.

A synthetic version of it is already covered: the `old-workflows` rehearsal fixture converges a member holding the previous workflow shape, and `engine-tests/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run-entry-shim.test.mjs` pins that the shim starts the run and that `scheduler-workflow-shape` accepts either spelling. What no test can show is a real member's scheduler workflow running green through it.

If this fails, every member in that window has a queue that has silently stopped — nothing instantiates standing items, nothing readies blocked ones, nothing reclaims a dead claim — with no run left to report it.

[{"id":5379959696,"body":"## Finding: the elimination premise does not survive contact with the files

I read every candidate site rather than working from the census summaries. **Close to none of the ~40–50 is safely eliminable.** The estimate in the issue body was derived from sweep summaries, which record *that* a pack asserts a GitHub fact but not *whether* the assertion is gratuitous. Reading them in context, almost every one is either already platform-neutral or load-bearing.

### Bucket 1 was largely a census artifact, not prose to fix

The sweeps counted the *concept* landing on Actions in practice, not GitHub vocabulary in the text. Checked line by line:

| Site | Text | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `firebase/skills/create-release-plan/SKILL.md:28,30` | "release-workflow variables", "the release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset" | already neutral |
| `macos/RULES.md:64,77` | "signing secrets being present", "in a build annotation" | already neutral |
| `spec-driven-product/RULES.md:56,127` | "gate the merge from CI", "cuts from `main`" | already neutral |
| `aws-sam/RULES.md:17` | "the last green deploy workflow" | already neutral |
| `web-scraping/RULES.md:59,154` | datacenter-IP blocks, commit-step durability | already neutral |
| `research-project/RULES.md:380` | "branch/commit/PR conventions" | cross-forge |

Genuine edits available: **1–2 marginal ones** (`firebase:50` "a workflow dispatch", `web-scraping:55` "repository secrets"), each worth one census point and each slightly *less* precise afterward. `macos/README.md:63` names GitHub Actions in a **provenance** note about a real project that genuinely used it — vaguening a factual attribution makes the doc worse, not more portable.

### Bucket 2: every candidate has a legitimate defense

- **Vendored stubs** (`chrome-extension`, `static-website` bump-version workflows) travel into member repos, where a canon reference dangles. Must stay self-contained.
- **Migration records** (`claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` ×2) are dated historical accounts. The canon says do not change historical records.
- **`task.md` files** (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `tidy-repo`, `jwt`, `product-wiki`) are read standalone by executor sessions.
- **The canary README** — the fact *is* the pack's reason to exist.
- **`claudinite-dashboard`** (`README.md:498`, `pack.mjs:37`) states the fact as the **premise** of a design decision (seed the workflow; follow the scheduler rather than `push`). It does not re-spell the withhold mechanism, and the canon rule permits A to say what it needs from B.
- **Squash-merge "restatements"** turned out not to exist: `basics` has none, and `tidy-repo/skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md:11` is a six-word parenthetical justifying its own decision rule.

### The always-loaded surface is already clean

`RULES.md` is the only text every session in every declaring repo pays for, and it is already lean: `tidy-repo/RULES.md` has **zero** GitHub mentions despite 11 credited assumptions (they live in skills and `task.mjs`, where they belong), and `basics/RULES.md`'s nine are the issue→branch→PR lifecycle itself, already delegating procedure to `git-github-advanced`.

### One genuinely ambiguous case, resolved against editing

`writing-tasks/SKILL.md:171` says `task.md` must state the **constraint** and drop the mechanism. The tracker cluster's "creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument" is mechanism by that reading — but it is precisely what stops a session collapsing the two calls into one. Dropping it trades a census point for a live failure mode.

### Recommendation

**Do not run the sweep.** Landing ~40 edits to hit a number would vaguen accurate provenance, weaken standalone-readable task specs, and rewrite historical migration records — a net loss against a metric that was never a cost. The ~200 inherent assumptions are what these packs *do*; the only real lever is a forge-abstraction seam, which #959's standing decision rejects absent a second consumer.

No code changes pushed. Awaiting a decision on whether to close this as not-planned.

- The `PACK_VERSIONED` fixture's legacy spelling in `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`, and the zero/legacy assertions in `engine-tests/version.test.mjs`.

Keep `parseVersion`'s treatment of **zero** — that is the install floor (`docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md` §3), not a legacy version.

{"number":1073,"title":"Move the Chrome Web Store release pipeline into Claudinite tasks","body":"Tracking issue. The `chrome-extension` pack ships the store release as five workflows plus three composite actions, with a `store-release` task that only *dispatches* them. Move the work itself into task code-work.

> ### ⛔ Blocked on #883
>
> **Do not start implementing anything.** #883 changes the queue-engine contract this plan is written against. Phase -1 below must complete first, and the revised plan needs owner approval before any code is written.

> **Body repaired 2026-08-20**, before any implementation, per `writing-migration-plans`. The original is archived in a comment below; the comment trail holds the derivation and the review that forced these changes. **From the first commit onward this body is append-only.**

Follows #1069 / #1071, which established that the grounds for keeping a workflow are narrower than the corpus claimed: an Actions-only secret is reachable from code-work (`required_secrets`), an OIDC identity is a `permissions:` line, and a one-shot external effect is `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`. The only surviving ground is the Actions **composition model** — a `uses:` step. In this pipeline that is exactly and only the Pages deploy.

## Owner decisions

1. **The privacy-page refresh leaves the release path.** It renders `PRIVACY.md`, which changes on its own schedule, not on every store publish. It gets its own trigger — and that is what removes the last `uses:` from the release path.
2. **Human "bump version" merges stay manual.** Today a bump merge cuts the GitHub Release but does **not** upload to the store; a human publishes deliberately. The daily patch auto-release remains the only automatic path to the store.
3. **`store-publish` reads the store** to decide whether the latest release is live, rather than inferring from the version diff.
4. **Member cleanup is done by a session** (route c). The general "no automation can retire a workflow it once delivered" gap stays unfiled; no pre-flight push.
5. **The bump lands as a self-merging PR**, not a push to main — via `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` → `land-pr.mjs`, under the member's own `maintenance.delivery`.

## End state — three atoms, plus the privacy page

One operation per task, chained by preconditions rather than by ordering edges or parameters. Each precondition becomes true *because the previous task produced its output*.

| task | frequency | precondition | does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `release-patch-bump` | daily | shipped paths changed since the latest release tag | patch bump, landed as a self-merging PR |
| `release-package` | manual | manifest version ahead of the latest release | build + cut the GitHub Release |
| `store-publish` | manual | the latest release is not live on the store | upload the prod zip |
| `privacy-page` | manual | `PRIVACY.md` touched, or woken | dispatch the Pages deploy |

The `manual` tasks are woken by the session that merges the bump PR — "bump version" lands via a normal PR and `LGTM` merges it in-session, so a witness is already present and no cadence is needed.

`on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` belongs on **`store-publish` alone** — the store upload is the one genuinely non-idempotent act. The decomposition makes every other stage self-healing: a torn run leaves the world in a state the next stage's precondition re-derives.

`expected_outcome: 'merged-pr'` on `release-patch-bump`. `required_secrets: ['CHROME_EXTENSION_ID', 'CHROME_CLIENT_ID', 'CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET', 'CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN']` on `store-publish`.

### What each piece becomes

| today | becomes |
|---|---|
| `chrome-extension-release.yml` (orchestrator) | deleted — the tasks own every trigger |
| `chrome-extension-daily-release.yml` | split across the three atoms |
| `chrome-extension-create-package.yml` | `release-package`'s worker |
| `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml` | `store-publish`'s worker |
| `deploy-privacy-page.yml` | survives, rewritten to be dispatchable; the one remaining `uses:` surface |
| `actions/read-release-config/`, `actions/bump-extension-patch/` | plain modules the workers import; the `action.yml` wrappers deleted |
| `actions/report-failure/` | deleted, with **no replacement** — a failing task parks `needs-human`, which is the error report |
| `release-workflows.mjs` conformance | mostly deleted; what remains guards `release.config`, not workflow shape |

## Phase -1 — revisit against #883 (blocking)

#883 implements the work-as-work amendments in `engine/scheduler/queue/`. Several of this plan's conclusions were reasoned against the pre-amendment contract and must be re-derived, not merely re-read.

- [ ] **Re-derive the leash conclusion.** The plan concluded "no split; `release-package` stays one task" from a 50-minute job budget shared across `maxItems` items. #883 retires `timeout-minutes ≤ leash` once heartbeat comments land, and re-sizes run timeouts to `maxItems` × the largest work bound. Long work stops being illegal, so the constraint that produced that conclusion no longer exists in the same form.
- [ ] **Re-derive the chain's latency.** The three atoms are chained by preconditions, each becoming true because the previous produced its output. Under today's engine each link waits a tick (~1h). #883's **self-re-dispatch** and **readiness re-check at close (F1)** are both aimed exactly at that — with them, the chain drains in one sitting. This changes whether the decomposition is cheap or expensive, and may change the `frequency` choices.
- [ ] **Re-check the `report-failure` deletion against the durable record.** #883 adds the `claudinite-task-exec` record plus artifact links to the terminal comment, noting that today *"an agentless run's only record expires with its Actions log."* All three release tasks are agentless. Confirm the park-plus-record is the whole replacement, since the deletion was decided before that record existed.
- [ ] **Account for the `prework` → work-step key rename.** #883 lists it as a fleet migration touching the vendored key in every member's task files, shipped with a compatibility window. Writing three new task declarations immediately before that rename means authoring them on vocabulary that is about to change; decide whether to wait, or to write them on the new key behind the compatibility window.
- [ ] **Re-check tick/drain decoupling against Phase 2.** The drain leaving the tick's concurrency group changes how a forced `wake` behaves during member verification.
- [ ] **Re-run the whole plan review** (the `writing-migration-plans` findings-by-cost sort) against the amended engine, then **get owner approval on the revised plan before any code is written.**

**Exit:** #883 closed, every box above answered in a comment on this issue, and the owner has approved the revised plan.

## Phase 0 — out-of-band setup

**Nothing outside the repo.** The four `CHROME_*` secrets already exist in member repos under these names; no new token grant (the executor already has `contents: write` and `actions: write`); Pages source unchanged.

There **is** a delivery dependency, but it is a Phase 2 entry condition rather than a human step — see Phase 2.

## Phase 1 — the PR stack (one review gate)

PRs 1–4 stacked, each based on the previous, reviewed together, merged base-first. **PR 5 is authored in the stack but held out of that merge** — it is destructive to the canon's own delivery surface, so it lands only after Phase 2 reads back true.

- [ ] **1. Two signal collectors, and `release.config` as a module.** Lift `read-config.mjs` out of the composite action. Add to the `release` collector: a `/compare/{latestTag}...{defaultBranch}` changed-files read, and a store live-version read. - [ ] Drive the pipeline on `missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`, waking each atom in turn.
      **Exit:** each task's item terminal, and the store shows a submission at the expected version.
- [ ] Repeat on `TLDR` and `CrosswordChat`.
      **Exit:** all three members' items terminal.

## Phase 3 — the tail (destructive; only after Phase 2 reads back true)

- [ ] Merge PR 5.
- [ ] Attach the three member repos to a session with push access; delete the four `chrome-extension-*` workflows and the three `.github/actions/` composites from each, one PR per repo.
      **Exit:** each member's `.github/workflows/` contains `deploy-privacy-page.yml` and no other `chrome-extension-*` file, and each member's next release item still converges terminal.

You are running the `single-issue-triage` skill from the missingbulb/Claudinite repo on a batch of open GitHub issues. This is part of an automated `tidy-issues` task run (item #1407) — no human is watching live.

Repo: missingbulb/Claudinite (use ONLY mcp__github__* MCP tools for GitHub access — no gh CLI).

Your batch — triage ONLY these issue numbers, nothing else: #590, #840, #996, #1003, #991, #766, #952, #223, #920

Local checkout: /home/user/Claudinite, currently checked out exactly at origin/main (commit 536d2fe2232d4243fd60af402255177d44cc7c42) — you can Read/Grep files there directly as ground truth for "is this implemented in main now". Do not run git commands that change the checkout.

## The triage skill (apply verbatim to each issue)

Triage each issue and take the FIRST applicable action:

1. **Already implemented in `main`** → close (state_reason: completed) + a one-line comment citing where in main it landed (file/path, not a guess). "Implemented in main" means the issue's actual ask is TRUE of main's CURRENT content, verified by reading the actual files/code — never inferred from a linked PR merging or the issue "looking done". If you can't point to the exact spot, do NOT close — comment instead saying what's still missing.

2. **Conflicts with a current guideline/convention in the repo** → add label `needs-decision` (create it if missing) + comment naming the conflict.

3. **Blocked by another open issue** → add label `blocked` + comment `blocked by #N`.

4. **Small and quick to do** → add label `quick-win` + comment scoping the work briefly.

5. **Else** → leave it alone, no action.

Every checkbox ticked in the issue body is a claim, not proof — it's your reason to go verify against main, never the answer itself. Verified true → close. Not verified → comment naming what's missing. A PARTIALLY ticked list is not a completion signal at all — treat as if it carried no boxes. Exception: if the ask has NO repo-side artifact (a console setting, something only a human can do), the author's own ticks ARE the closing condition — say so and close.

## Never repeat a verdict

Before acting on an issue, read its comments (mcp__github__issue_read method get_comments). Find the most recent comment that ends with a marker line `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=... -->`. If the action you're about to take is the SAME action that comment already announced, do NOTHING for that issue (post no comment, change no label) — record it as `unchanged`.

Every comment you post must end, alone on the last line, with:
```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```
where `<action>` is one of: closed, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win.

## Hard bounds

- This task writes ISSUES ONLY. Never open, close, merge, or comment on a pull request.
- Only touch the 9 issue numbers listed above. Do not look at or act on any other issue.
- If an issue is already closed or otherwise not open, skip it and note why — take no action.

## What to report back

For EACH of the 9 issue numbers, report one line: `#N: <action> — <one-sentence reason>`, where action is one of: closed, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, left, unchanged, skipped(<reason>). Keep the whole report under 400 words total.

{"number":748,"title":"conformance-backlog: committed-build-artifact check (promote cannot land a check — fixtures sit outside its write surface)","body":"Two things, from the 2026-08-11 `canon-curation/growth-promote` run (#745, PR #747).

## 1. A structural block: promote's ladder cannot reach the check rung

`growth-promote`'s task spec says a lesson a check can carry is **authored as the check** in the promote PR — "the rule module in the right pack, the failure message carrying the generalized lesson, **plus a fixture test proving it fires**".

That is mechanically impossible today:

- promote's write surface is bounded to `packs/` and `skills/`, enforced by `.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/promote-scope.mjs` on the `growth-promote` branch prefix;
- a canon pack's fixture test lives under `packs-tests/`, which is **outside** that surface;
- and it cannot move into `packs/` either — `.github/workflows/ci.yml` pins a closed set of test roots (`engine-tests/`, `packs-tests/`, `vendoring/`, `dev/tools/`, `.claudinite/local/packs/`), with `engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs` failing on any tracked test outside them.

So every promote run must fall back to prose for a convertible rule, and the "prose is the fallback, not the default" ladder never fires. Whichever way it is resolved (widen `inBounds` to `packs-tests/`, or add `packs/` as a test root), it is an owner decision — the run declined to widen its own gate.

## 2. The conversion this blocked

The `.gitignore`-pruning lesson (LaughCounter's local pack, promoted as prose to `git-github-advanced` in #747) converts to a world-scope `basics` check. Written and green locally before being pulled:

- **`packs/basics/committed-build-artifact.mjs`** — advisory, relevance-first. Flags a *tracked* file matching a confined set of artifacts no project tracks on purpose: `__pycache__/`, `*.py[co]`, `.pytest_cache/`, `.mypy_cache/`, `.ruff_cache/`, `*.egg-info/`, `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`. The `fix` line carries the lesson (delete the artifacts before dropping their ignore rules; read `git diff --cached --stat` after a bulk `git add -A`).
- **`packs-tests/basics/committed-build-artifact.test.mjs`** — four cases: clean tree silent; a swept-in `__pycache__` found; the tool-cache/OS set found; and a narrowness case proving silence on deliberately vendored trees (`node_modules/`, `dist/`, `build/`) and on prose merely naming `__pycache__`.

Advisory rather than blocking on purpose: the fix is a deletion, and pre-existing junk in a member repo should surface as a finding to clear, not red that repo's sweep and block its maintenance PR.

The set was chosen so the check stays inert on anything a repo might legitimately vendor; `node_modules/` and `dist/` are deliberately excluded.

Refs #745.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/single-issue-triage

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```

{"number":1072,"title":"Production code must not reference its tests — land it as a check","body":"Owner decision while landing #1066: **there shouldn't be references to tests from production code.** That change removed the four citations it created; the rule itself is still unwritten, and eleven pre-existing sites still cross the line.

## The rule

A shipping `.mjs` under `packs/` or `engine/` must not name a `*.test.mjs` path. It is deterministic, so it belongs on the ladder as a **check**, not prose — the assurance authored and seen to fail before the sites are cleaned.

Documentation is a separate question and probably outside it: `engine/checks/README.md` describing where a pack's tests live, or `.github/workflows/ci.yml` naming test globs, is the corpus documenting itself, not production code pointing at its own test.

## The sites as of today

```
engine/checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs:103
engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs:72
engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs:3
engine/scheduler/run.mjs:10
engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs:35
engine/scheduler/slots.mjs:18
packs/claudinite-dashboard/model.mjs:11
packs/claudinite-dashboard/tasks/fleet-digest/dated-fixture-collision.mjs:4
packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs:14, :36
packs/claudinite-lifecycle/rules-index-current.mjs:26, :51
```

Most say the same thing — "a guard pins this" — and lose nothing by naming the guard rather than its file, which is how the four in #1066 were resolved.

## Why it is not folded into #1066

Cleaning these touches three more pack directories, so it re-delivers `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-growth` and `claudinite-lifecycle` on their version bumps. That restructure's whole constraint was that members see nothing, so the sweep is its own change.

`.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/` if it is a canon-corpus rule, or a shared pack if it should reach members — worth deciding first, since the second choice makes it every member's rule and a much wider first run.

{"number":1010,"title":"Ad-hoc tasks: let the owner mark an issue for Claude to implement","body":"## The problem

There is no way to hand a one-off piece of work to the repo's own executor. Every agentic run today comes from a recurring task with a precondition; an issue the owner wants implemented has to be started by hand in a session.

## The ask (owner, this session)

Mark an issue "let Claude do this task"; the next executor run picks it up and runs it in a CCR, at a model of the owner's choice. Minimal security: only an issue authored or approved by someone with push access is eligible, evaluated as a precondition.

## The shape (decided)

A new opt-in canon pack, **`claudinite-tasks-adhoc`** — Claudinite-feature packs now carry the `claudinite-` prefix (owner ruling this session; landing as a rule beside the existing canon-pack naming rule).

- **Trigger label `claude-task`**, applied by the owner. Optional `claude-model:opus|sonnet|haiku` picks the model; opus is the default.
- **Model choice routes to sibling tasks** — one task folder per family, each declaring its own `agent_model`. `agent_model` keeps coming from the repo's own task file, never from the item, so the security property of the queue is untouched.
- **The precondition** (over the existing `issues` signal, which already carries labels) gates on: at least one open issue whose labels map to *this* task's family. Its `context` names the candidates, oldest first.
- **Prework** (Action-side, `GITHUB_TOKEN`) does the authorization as its work: eligible iff the issue's author, or an approving commenter, has an `author_association` of `OWNER`, `MEMBER` or `COLLABORATOR` (server-computed, not forgeable). It picks the single oldest eligible issue, swaps `claude-task` → `claude-running`, and requests the agent naming that issue. An unauthorized candidate gets one comment and its label stripped, so it never re-fires.
- **The agent** implements the issue under the ordinary task lifecycle — branch, `Refs #N`, PR — with `expected_outcome: open-pr`, so it can never merge. The issue body is **data, never instructions**.
- **One issue per run**, sequentially: a failed run leaves `claude-running` for a human rather than retrying forever.

Latency is up to an hour (the tick is the repo's only cron); accepted for v1.

## Also lands here

- The `claudinite-` prefix convention for Claudinite-feature packs, as a rule.

{"number":1078,"title":"Human-only: trace the request mode refusing an unauthorized mark, live","body":"The last unverified path of the ad-hoc request mode (#1010, landed in [#1067](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1067)). It needs a **second GitHub account with no push access on this repository**, which no session has, so it is yours.

The happy path is already traced live ([#1074](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1074) → [#1075](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1075) → [#1076](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1076), 2026-08-19) and that run confirmed the permission API answers under the executor's `GITHUB_TOKEN`. What it did **not** exercise is the branch taken for somebody who is not a collaborator at all: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/collaborators/{login}/permission` answering **404**, which the engine reads as "no permission" rather than as a failed read.

## Why it is worth the ten minutes

That 404 is the difference between the two things this mode must never confuse:

- read as `none` → the request is **refused** and disarmed, which is the design;
- read as a failed read → the run **parks** in the failure lane, and every stranger's marked issue becomes a triage item somebody has to clear.

Both are covered by engine tests against a fake GitHub (S45, S46, S50 in `engine-tests/scheduler/queue/request-mode.test.mjs`). Neither has been seen against the real API, and the two differ by one status code.

## Steps

- [ ] **From the second account** (no push access here), open a throwaway issue — anything, one line. *While this is off: nothing to mark.*
- [ ] **From your own account**, apply `claude-task` to it. Applying the mark to somebody else's issue is meant to authorize nothing — that is the point of the trace. *While this is off: the tick has nothing to adopt.*
- [ ] **Run the tick** — wait for the hourly one, or dispatch [Claudinite scheduler](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml) with no inputs. *While this is off: the mark just sits there.*
- [ ] **Watch, on the throwaway issue**: one comment beginning "Not implementing this:", `claude-queued` removed, **no session started**. And on the work item the tick created: closed, `task:obsolete`.
- [ ] **Watch the next tick or two**: nothing re-adopts it. The disarm is what stops the refusal repeating forever.
- [ ] **Second variant, same issue**: have the second account comment `/claude go`, re-apply `claude-task`, run the tick. It must refuse again — the phrase decides nothing; the permission behind it does.
- [ ] **Positive control**: comment `/claude go` yourself, re-apply `claude-task`, run the tick. This one must run. (Skip if you would rather not spend a session; the happy path is already traced.)

## Closing condition

Both refusals observed, with the item numbers linked here, and the throwaway issue closed. If either refusal instead **parks** the item at `task:needs-human-failure`, do not close this — the 404 is being read as a failed read, and the fix is in the `request` collector's `permissionOf` (`engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs`).

You are running the `single-issue-triage` skill from the missingbulb/Claudinite repo on a batch of open GitHub issues. This is part of an automated `tidy-issues` task run (item #1407) — no human is watching live.

Repo: missingbulb/Claudinite (use ONLY mcp__github__* MCP tools for GitHub access — no gh CLI).

Your batch — triage ONLY these issue numbers, nothing else: #923, #942, #926, #239, #841, #409, #498

Local checkout: /home/user/Claudinite, currently checked out exactly at origin/main (commit 536d2fe2232d4243fd60af402255177d44cc7c42) — you can Read/Grep files there directly as ground truth for "is this implemented in main now". Do not run git commands that change the checkout.

## The triage skill (apply verbatim to each issue)

Triage each issue and take the FIRST applicable action:

1. **Already implemented in `main`** → close (state_reason: completed) + a one-line comment citing where in main it landed (file/path, not a guess). "Implemented in main" means the issue's actual ask is TRUE of main's CURRENT content, verified by reading the actual files/code — never inferred from a linked PR merging or the issue "looking done". If you can't point to the exact spot, do NOT close — comment instead saying what's still missing.

2. **Conflicts with a current guideline/convention in the repo** → add label `needs-decision` (create it if missing) + comment naming the conflict.

3. **Blocked by another open issue** → add label `blocked` + comment `blocked by #N`.

4. **Small and quick to do** → add label `quick-win` + comment scoping the work briefly.

5. **Else** → leave it alone, no action.

Every checkbox ticked in the issue body is a claim, not proof — it's your reason to go verify against main, never the answer itself. Verified true → close. Not verified → comment naming what's missing. A PARTIALLY ticked list is not a completion signal at all — treat as if it carried no boxes. Exception: if the ask has NO repo-side artifact (a console setting, something only a human can do), the author's own ticks ARE the closing condition — say so and close.

## Never repeat a verdict

Before acting on an issue, read its comments (mcp__github__issue_read method get_comments). Find the most recent comment that ends with a marker line `<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=... -->`. If the action you're about to take is the SAME action that comment already announced, do NOTHING for that issue (post no comment, change no label) — record it as `unchanged`.

Every comment you post must end, alone on the last line, with:
```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```
where `<action>` is one of: closed, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win.

## Hard bounds

- This task writes ISSUES ONLY. Never open, close, merge, or comment on a pull request.
- Only touch the 9 issue numbers listed above. Do not look at or act on any other issue.
- If an issue is already closed or otherwise not open, skip it and note why — take no action.

## What to report back

For EACH of the 9 issue numbers, report one line: `#N: <action> — <one-sentence reason>`, where action is one of: closed, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, left, unchanged, skipped(<reason>). Keep the whole report under 400 words total.

{"number":590,"title":"Adoption never sets the two repo settings baselining depends on — add them to bootstrap (both are scriptable)","body":"Baselining's delivery depends on two repository settings that **nothing in adoption ever sets, checks, or mentions**. `packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md` has zero references to either — the only mentions anywhere in the corpus are the error strings added by #585.

Both are the direct cause of the two-day fleet stall.

## The settings

| Setting | UI | API |
|---|---|---|
| Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests | Settings → Actions → General | `PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/permissions/workflow` → `{"can_approve_pull_request_reviews": true}` |
| Allow auto-merge | Settings → General → Pull Requests | `PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}` → `{"allow_auto_merge": true}` |

**Both are readable and writable by script** — plain REST, no UI-only step. The matching `GET` on each returns the current value, so a conformance check could assert them rather than only bootstrap setting them.

The constraint is the credential, not the API: both require **admin** on the repo. The Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot do it, so this cannot be self-healed by baselining from inside the member. It belongs to either:

- **adoption** (`adopt-claudinite`), which already runs in a session with the owner's own credentials, or
- **the sheepdog pack**, whose `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` spans the account — it could converge both settings fleet-wide alongside `fleet-freshness`, and would catch a repo whose settings were later flipped back.

The second is the stronger option: adoption sets it once, whereas the sheepdog sweep keeps it true.

## Why it matters

Without the first, the maintenance PR is never created (#585 — silent before that fix, loud after). Without the second, an `auto-merge` member's PR opens and never lands. Neither is visible from inside the member repo, and neither produced any signal until it was investigated by hand.

## Suggested scope

1. Adoption sets both over the owner's credentials, and records what it set.
2. A check (or the sheepdog freshness sweep) asserts both remain true, reporting the exact API path when they are not.
3. `adopt-claudinite` documents them, so a hand-adopted repo does not silently miss them.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/590","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["quick-win"],"assignees":[],"comments":4,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-07-30T21:42:38Z","updated_at":"2026-08-19T05:18:54Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}
